A theorem of Retakh for exact ∞ \infty -categories and higher extension functors
Erlend D. Børve, Paul Trygsland

Abstract
. We define extension ∞ \infty -categories for exact ∞ \infty -categories in terms of bifibrations. Extension ∞ \infty -categories are invariant when passing to the stable hull, and consequently we show that they form an Ω \Omega -spectrum, generalizing a theorem of Retakh. Finally, we show that the homotopy groups of extension ∞ \infty -categories are naturally isomorphic to the higher extension groups of the extriangulated category given by the homotopy category.



2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
14F35,18E10,18G30

0.
Introduction

Boardman–Vogt introduced the homotopy invariant structures known as
\infty
-categories in the early 1970s
[
7
]
. Their motivation was to develop a machinery for better understanding infinite loop spaces, or “homotopy abelian groups.” A central idea is to avoid choices for compositions, but rather have a space encoding all possible choices. As an example, a loop space does not carry a natural well-defined concatenation of loops before applying
\pi_{0}
, though it is weakly homotopy equivalent to a topological group
[
1
, p. 31]
. Nowadays, it is well-known that
\infty
-categories serve as a model for
(\infty,1)
–categories
[
15
,
20
]
.

Roughly speaking, an exact category
\mathcal{C}
is an additive category together with a collection of short exact sequences subject to certain constraints
[
14
]
, (Keller’s axioms
[
17
]
can be taken as a modern approach). This allows for homological algebra to be performed in a more general context than abelian categories. Non-abelian examples include the category of vector bundles of a scheme and the category of Banach spaces. In addition to homological algebra, exact categories provide a natural framework for
\mathrm{K}
-theory. Quillen introduced the higher algebraic
\mathrm{K}
–groups in this context
[
27
]
.

Barwick defines exact
\infty
-categories in order to generalise definitions and results in
\mathrm{K}
-theory
[
3
,
4
,
5
]
. This broadens the scope considerably; it captures both (nerves of) exact categories and stable
\infty
-categories. Moreover, every extension closed subcategory of a stable
\infty
-category has the structure of an exact
\infty
-category. In fact, all exact
\infty
-categories occur in this manner; Klemenc shows that all exact
\infty
-categories can be embedded into a stable hull
[
18
]
. One would thus expect more constructions and results about exact categories to generalise, paving the way for potentially useful applications. In particular, one could study homological algebra from an
\infty
-categorical point of view.

To better understand the homological algebra of exact
\infty
-categories
\mathscr{C}
, we define
\infty
-categorical analogues of extension categories, denoted by
\Extcat^{n}_{\mathscr{C}}(b,a)
, where
a
and
b
are objects in
\mathscr{C}
. These generalise the well-established extension categories for exact categories. It is well-known that the Yoneda Ext-groups
\Ext^{n}_{\mathcal{C}}(b,a)
of an exact category
\mathcal{C}
can be recovered as the zeroth homotopy groups of
\Extcat^{n}_{\mathcal{C}}(b,a)

[
23
, Proposition XII.4.4]
.

To modernise the notion of extension (
\infty
-)category, we use the language of bifibrations (
Definition

2.1
).
For an exact
\infty
-category
\mathscr{C}
, we declare that
\Extcat^{0}_{\mathscr{C}}(b,a)\coloneqq\hom_{\mathscr{C}}(b,a)
, the mapping space from
b
to
a
. More precisely, we define
\Extcat^{0}_{\mathscr{C}}
to be the mapping space bifibration of
\mathscr{C}
. The first extension bifibration
\Extcat^{1}_{\mathscr{C}}
is defined analogously to its
1
-categorical counterpart, and the higher one are obtained by compositions of
\Extcat^{1}_{\mathscr{C}}
with itself.

The main result of ours is the following.

Theorem
3.3
.

Let
\mathscr{C}
be an exact
\infty
-category and let
\Sp
be the
\infty
-category of
\Omega
-spectrum objects. There exists a functor

such that the
n
-th component of the spectrum
\Extcat_{\mathscr{C}}(b,a)
is weakly equivalent to the extension
\infty
-category
\Extcat^{n}_{\mathscr{C}}(b,a)
for all
a,b\in\mathscr{C}
.

We deduce that the spectrum

\Extcat_{\mathscr{C}}(b,a)\coloneqq\{\Extcat^{n}_{\mathscr{C}}(b,a)\}_{n\geq 0}

is an
\Omega
-spectrum. This is a generalisation of a theorem of Retakh, who proved the same result for abelian categories
[
28
, Theorem 2(b)]
. It follows that we have isomorphisms

(0.b)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{-n}\Extcat_{\mathscr{C}}(b,a)\simeq\pi_{0}\Extcat^{n}_{\mathscr{C}}(b,a)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{1}\Extcat^{n+1}_{\mathscr{C}}(b,a)}

of homotopy groups. This means, in particular, that the higher structure of
\Extcat_{\mathscr{C}}(b,a)
descends to the abelian group structure on classical
\Ext
-groups.

To prove Theorem
3.3
, we show that the extension categories
\Extcat^{n}_{\mathscr{C}}(b,a)
are weakly homotopy equivalent to
\map_{\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{st}}_{\geq 0}(\mathscr{C})}(b,\Sigma^{n}a)
, where
\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{st}}_{\geq 0}(\mathscr{C})
is a certain subcategory of the stable hull of
\mathscr{C}
. The Retakh-esque spectra of extension
\infty
-categories will be weakly equivalent to Lurie’s mapping spectra in the prestable
\infty
-category
\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{st}}_{\geq 0}(\mathscr{C})
.

There is a notion extriangulated categories, defined by Nakaoka–Palu
[
24
]
, which simultaneously generalises exact and triangulated categories. Recently, Nakaoka–Palu showed that the homotopy category of an exact
\infty
-category has a natural extriangulated structure
[
25
, Theorem 4.22]
. In particular, it encapsulates the now well-known result that the homotopy category of a stable
\infty
-category is canonically triangulated
[
21
, Theorem 1.1.2.14]
, and moreover the homotopy category of the nerve of an exact category is obviously exact.

For a non-negative integer
n
, Gorsky–Nakaoka–Palu
[
13
, Definition 3.1]
define the
n
-extension groups for extriangulated categories, ultimately inspired by Yoneda’s classic monograph on extension categories
[
31
]
. We show that the higher structure contained in the Retakh spectra
\Extcat_{\mathscr{C}}(-,-)
descends to the
n
-extension groups in the homotopy category.

Theorem
4.8
.

Let
\mathscr{C}
be an exact
\infty
-category. Then the bifunctors
\pi_{0}\Extcat^{n}_{\mathscr{C}}(-,-)
on the extriangulated category
(\homcat\mathscr{C},\pi_{0}\Extcat^{1}_{\mathscr{C}}(-,-))
is naturally isomorphic to the
n
-th extension functor of
\homcat\mathscr{C}
.

Outline.
Section
1
contains little to no original ideas. It is concerned with basics of exact
\infty
-categories and diagram lemmas. We define extension categories for
\infty
-categories in Section
2
.
Theorem

3.3
is stated and proved in Section
3
. In the final Section
4
, we discuss how Retakh spectra determine the higher structure of the extriangulation on homotopy categories. In particular, Theorem
4.8
is proven.

Notation and conventions.
Throughout, we fix a Grothendieck universe
U
. Simplicial sets should thus be understood as simplicial
U
-sets. We refer to Shulman
[
29
, Section 8]
for a detailed treatment of Grothendieck universes.

A category
J
will be identified with its nerve
\mathrm{N}(J)
, so that it can be regarded as an
\infty
-category. An
\infty
-functor between
\infty
-categories
\mathscr{C}
and
\mathscr{D}
(i.e. a morphism of the underlying simplicial sets) will simply be referred to as a functor.

The
0
-simplices of an
\infty
-category
\mathscr{C}
are often referred to as objects. Similarly,
1
-simplices are referred to as maps or morphisms.
We write
f\sim g
when the 1-simplicies
f
and
g
are homotopic. A degenerate 1-simplex
s_{0}X
, or a map which is homotopic to it, is denoted by
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
.

For two simplicial sets
X
and
Y

\map(X,Y)

n
-simplices is
\map(X,Y)_{n}={\sSet}(X\times[n],Y)
. Note that this space models the homotopy function complex
[
11
]
.

, where
\mathscr{C}
is an
\infty
-category, there is the subcomplex

A
biproduct
of a family
\{X_{i}\}_{i\in I}
of objects in
\mathscr{C}
is both a product and a coproduct of this family. If it exists, it will be denoted by
\bigoplus\limits_{i\in I}X_{i}
.

Let
\bigoplus\limits_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}
and
\bigoplus\limits_{j=1}^{m}Y_{j}

\mathscr{C}

1.
Exact
\infty
-categories

We first review exact
\infty
-categories, a generalisation of exact categories to the realm of
\infty
-categories.
Since the underlying category of an exact category is additive, it is only sensible to introduce the
\infty
-categorical notion.

Definition 1.1

(
[
3
, §2]
)
.

An
\infty
-category
\mathscr{C}
is
additive
if the following hold.

(Add1)

There is a zero object 0 in
\mathscr{C}
, which is to say that
\map_{\mathscr{C}}(0,x)
and
\map_{\mathscr{C}}(x,0)
are contractible for all
x\in\mathscr{C}
.

(Add2)

Finite products and coproducts exist in
\mathscr{C}
.

(Add3)

For any finite family of objects
\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\}
, the natural map

\coprod_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}\mathchoice{\hskip 2.15277pt\hbox to17.62pt{\vbox to13.73pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 0.2pt\lower-3.42159pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}
{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}}{{}}{}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}{}{}{{{}{}}}{}{}{{{}{}}}{}{}{}{}{{}}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 4.77 L 22.45 4.77}{fill:none} {{}{{}}{}{}{{}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{16.22218pt}{3.44443pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-dasharray,stroke-dashoffset} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-linejoin} \lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 1.11 0 C -0.28 0.28 -1.66 0.83 -3.32 1.8 C -1.66 0.55 -1.66 -0.55 -3.32 -1.8 C -1.66 -0.83 -0.28 -0.28 1.11 0 Z}{} \lxSVG@closescope \lxSVG@closescope }}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{
{}{}}}{
{}{}}

(Add4)

For all
x,y\in\mathscr{C}_{0}
, the Hom-set
\hom_{h\mathscr{C}}(x,y)\coloneqq\pi_{0}\map_{\mathscr{C}}(x,y)
admits an abelian group structure, where we define
f+g
to be the composite
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x\coprod x}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y\prod y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{pmatrix}1\\
1\end{pmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{pmatrix}f&0\\
0&g\end{pmatrix}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\begin{pmatrix}1&1\end{pmatrix}}

in
\homcat\mathscr{C}
.

A bicomplete
\infty
-category
\mathscr{C}
is additive precisely when the homotopy category
\homcat\mathscr{C}
is additive as an ordinary category. Analogously to how biproducts arise in additive categories, the axioms
(Add2)
and
(Add3)
imply that
\mathscr{C}
has finite biproducts.

Barwick defines exact
\infty
-categories
[
3
, Definition 3.1]
by adapting Keller’s minimal set of axioms
[
17
]
to the
\infty
-categorical setting.

Definition 1.2
.

Let
\mathscr{C}
be an additive
\infty
-category and let
\mathscr{C}_{{\dagger}}
and
\mathscr{C}^{{\dagger}}
be subcategories that contain all objects in
\mathscr{C}
, as well as all homotopy equivalences. The maps in
\mathscr{C}_{{\dagger}}
will be referred to as
cofibrations
, whereas morphisms in
\mathscr{C}^{{\dagger}}
are
fibrations
. The triple
(\mathscr{C},\mathscr{C}_{{\dagger}},\mathscr{C}^{{\dagger}})
is called an
exact
\infty
-category
if the following axioms hold.

(Ex1)

For any zero object
0
in
\mathscr{C}_{0}

(Ex2)

Pushouts of cofibrations exist and are cofibrations, and dually for pullbacks of fibrations.

(Ex3)

The following are equivalent for a homotopy coherent square
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}

(Ex3.1)

The square is a pullback, the map
g
is a cofibration and
p
is a fibration.

(Ex3.2)

The square is a pushout, the map
i
is a cofibration and
f
is a fibration.

If the subcategories
\mathscr{C}_{{\dagger}}
and
\mathscr{C}^{{\dagger}}
are implicitly specified, we simply say that
\mathscr{C}
is exact. A triple
(\mathscr{C},\mathscr{C}_{{\dagger}},\mathscr{C}^{{\dagger}})
satisfying the axioms above is called an
exact structure
on
\mathscr{C}
. Whenever a cofibration appears in a diagram, it will be drawn as follows:
(like a monomorphism in an ordinary category). A fibration will be drawn as a two-headed arrow
.

Nerves of exact categories are exact
\infty
-categories, where the class of cofibrations consists of the admissible monomorphisms, and the fibrations are the admissible epimorphisms. Moreover, any stable
\infty
-category
[
21
, Definition 1.1.1.9]
can be seen as an exact
\infty
-category where
\mathscr{C}_{{\dagger}}=\mathscr{C}=\mathscr{C}^{{\dagger}}
.

The axioms above provide a framework for exact sequences, in more or less the usual fashion.

Definition 1.3
.

Let
\mathscr{C}
be an exact
\infty
-category. An
exact sequence
in
\mathscr{C}
is a square
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}

where
0
is a zero object and the equivalent criteria in
(Ex3)
are met.

Equivalently, the exact sequences are bicartesian squares of the form
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\square}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

As is conventional for exact 1-categories, exact sequences can be drawn horizontally

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b,}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

omitting the zero object. There is not really any loss of information in such notation, as the choice of morphisms to/from zero is irrelevant up to homotopy.

Definition 1.4
.

A
map of exact sequences
is simply a map of bicartesian squares.
Such maps will mostly be depicted as homotopy commutative diagrams of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p^{\prime}}

Exact functors also have a completely analogous definition.

When checking that a functor is exact, one may equivalently consider the dual statement for fibrations
[
3
, Proposition 4.8]
. Exact sequences are obviously preserved by exact functors, and by considering split exact sequences one proves that they preserve the additive structure as well.

Full subcategories
\mathscr{D}
of a given exact
\infty
-category
\mathscr{C}
inherit the exact structure if they are
closed under extensions
, i.e. for all exact sequences
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}

with
a,b\in\mathscr{D}
, we have that
e\in\mathscr{D}
. The class of cofibrations in
\mathscr{D}

\mathscr{C}_{{\dagger}}\cap\mathscr{D}

\mathscr{D}

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\hskip 0.86108pt}\mathscr{C}

is then exact.

It turns out that all exact
\infty
-categories occur as extension closed subcategories of stable
\infty
-categories.

Theorem 1.6

(
[
18
, Theorem 1.2]
)
.

Given a small exact
\infty
-category
\mathscr{C}
, there exists a stable hull
\mathcal{H}^{\rm st}(\mathscr{C})
into which
\mathscr{C}
embeds exactly and universally.

We will reveal some of the structure of
\mathcal{H}^{\rm st}(\mathscr{C})
when we need it in Section
3
.
Theorem

1.6
can be seen as an
\infty
-categorical version of the Gabriel–Quillen embedding theorem for exact categories, which states that they embed exactly into abelian categories.

A number of results concerning exact
\infty
-categories generalise to exact
\infty
-categories. We will make frequent use of our next lemma, first generalised by Barwick.

Lemma 1.7

(
[
3
, Lemma 4.5]
)
.

A homotopy coherent square
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}

in an exact
\infty
-category is bicartesian if either of the following conditions holds.

(1)

The square is a pushout and
i
is a cofibration.

(2)

The square is a pullback and
p
is a fibration.

Generalisations of celebrated diagram lemmas will also be helpful in later sections. The first relates pushouts to maps of exact sequences.

Lemma 1.8

(
[
18
, Proposition A.1]
)
.

A pushout
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ulcorner}

where
i
is cofibration, can be extended to a map of exact sequences
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ulcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

Conversely, the existence of such a map of exact sequences implies that the square is a pushout. A dual statement holds for pullbacks along fibrations.

Secondly, a map of exact sequences has a canonical factorisation.

Lemma 1.9

(
[
18
, Proposition A.2]
)
.

Any map of exact sequences
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces d}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i_{a}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{b}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i_{c}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{d}}

can be factored
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces d}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i_{a}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\square}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{b}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\square}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i_{c}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{d}}

where the squares marked by
\square
are bicartesian.

The renowned Five Lemma is a consequence of
Lemma

1.9
. It will be proven in
Appendix

A
, since there is no significant difference from the special case of exact 1-categories.

Lemma 1.10

(Five lemma)
.

Consider a map of exact sequences
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces d}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i_{a}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{b}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i_{c}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{d}}

If
f^{\prime}
and
f^{\prime\prime}
are homotopy equivalences (resp. cofibrations, resp. fibrations), so is
f
.

As a curiosity, we also lift the
3\times 3
-lemma to the
\infty
-categorical setting. This proof is also deferred to
Appendix

A
.

Lemma 1.11

(
3\times 3
–lemma)
.

Consider the homotopy coherent diagram with exact columns
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a^{\prime\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e^{\prime\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b^{\prime\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i_{a}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i_{e}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i_{b}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{a}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{e}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{b}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g^{\prime\prime}}

If the middle row and one of the other rows are exact, then the remaining row is exact.

2.
\infty
-categories of extensions

Fix an exact
\infty
-category
\mathscr{C}
. We will generalise MacLane’s notion of extension category
[
23
]
to the
\infty
-categorical setting using modern techniques. Specifically, our constructions are defined in terms of bifibrations
[
20
, §2.4.7]
. Since bifibrations specify bifunctors, we will arrive at a definition of extension bifunctors for exact
\infty
-categories.

Let us first recall the definition of a bifibration.

A composite of inner fibrations is still an inner fibration
[
22
,
Tag 01BH
]
, whence we can complete the first step of the proof by recalling that
\epsilon_{1}
is the composite of the two inner fibrations displayed above.

Suppose that the solid part of the following diagram commutes
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Lambda^{m}_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Extcat^{1}_{\mathscr{C}}(\mathscr{C},\mathscr{C})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta^{m}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{C}\times\mathscr{C}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gamma}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\epsilon_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces s}

where the first
1
-simplex in
s
has a degenerate
1
-simplex as its second component. For
\epsilon_{1}
to be a bifibration, the dashed morphism should exist, rendering the whole diagram commutative.
There is also a dual horn filling requirement for
\Lambda^{m}_{m}
which is proved by dualising the reasoning in the next paragraphs.

The case
m=1
reduces to completing a diagram
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

to a map of exact sequences (Definition
1.4
). We need only compute the pushout of
i
along
f
and invoke Lemma
1.8
. The 1-simplex in
\Extcat_{\mathscr{C}}^{1}(\mathscr{C},\mathscr{C})
given by the dashed morphism will be
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\square}

The case
n\geq 2
is also a consequence of Lemma
1.8
. Indeed, the first
1
-simplex in
\gamma
is of the form
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b_{0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e_{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b_{0}}

whence the leftmost square is a pushout square due to Lemma
1.8
. A lift of
s
to
\Extcat^{1}_{\mathscr{C}}(\mathscr{C},\mathscr{C})
can now be constructed using the fact that pushout squares are initial in the category of cocones.
∎

Remark 2.3
.

For each pair of objects
a,b\in\mathscr{C}
, we deduce from
Proposition

2.2
that
\Extcat_{\mathscr{C}}^{1}(b,a)
is a Kan complex. One can also prove this assertion using the Five Lemma (
Lemma

1.10
). Indeed, the Five Lemma proves that all maps in
\Extcat_{\mathscr{C}}^{1}(b,a)
are homotopy equivalences, whence is it a Kan complex
[
15
, Corollary 1.4]
.

The higher extension bifibrations are defined by compositing the bifibration
\epsilon_{1}
with itself. Ayala–Francis devise composition procedure for bifibrations, rephrased here as
Lemma

2.4
. It uses the notion of localisation
[
9
, §7.1]

[
12
,
10
]
. The
Dwyer–Kan localisation
of a simplicial set
{X}
with respect to a set of maps
{W}\subseteq{X}
is given by the map
\ell_{W}
in the following diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{W}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Ex^{\infty}{W}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X}[{W}^{-1}]}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ulcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell_{{W}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}

where the square is a pushout, and the map
r
is a fibrant replacement in the Joyal model structure on simplicial sets. (Note that if
X
is an
\infty
-category, one can choose
r
to be the identity.)
Here,
\Ex^{\infty}
is the transfinite composite of Kan’s Ex-functor, which is the right adjoint of the barycentric subdivision functor
[
16
]
. It is well-known that
\Ex^{\infty}
is an endofunctor on the
\infty
-category of simplicial sets with essential image in the
\infty
-category of Kan complexes. Moreover, the unit

Such a map is a weak equivalence provided that
\alpha
and
\beta
are invertible.

We should justify why our construction generalises MacLane’s definition of extension categories for exact 1-categories. For any exact
\infty
-category
\mathscr{C}
, define
\classExtcat^{n}_{\mathscr{C}}(\mathscr{C},\mathscr{C})
by
\Extcat^{n}_{\mathscr{C}}(\mathscr{C},\mathscr{C})
for
n\leq 1
. The higher classical extension categories are recursively defined as pullbacks:

\classExtcat^{n}_{\mathscr{C}}(\mathscr{C},\mathscr{C})\coloneqq\classExtcat^{n-1}_{\mathscr{C}}(\mathscr{C},\mathscr{C})\times_{\mathscr{C}}\classExtcat^{1}_{\mathscr{C}}(\mathscr{C},\mathscr{C})

Given
a,b\in\mathscr{C}
, one defines
\classExtcat_{\mathscr{C}}^{n}(b,a)
in a similar manner as
\Extcat_{\mathscr{C}}^{n}(b,a)
. If
\mathscr{C}
is the nerve of an exact 1-category, then
\classExtcat_{\mathscr{C}}^{n}(b,a)
becomes equivalent to a classical extension category.

We point out that
\Extcat^{n}_{\mathscr{C}}(b,a)
will not be equivalent to MacLane’s extension category
\classExtcat_{\mathscr{C}}^{n}(b,a)
in general. In MacLane’s setup, the higher extension categories (i.e. for
n\geq 2
) need not be Kan complexes. However, we will show in
Proposition

2.5
that
\Extcat^{n}_{\mathscr{C}}(b,a)
is homotopy equivalent to
\classExtcat_{\mathscr{C}}^{n}(b,a)
.

Proposition 2.5
.

If
\mathscr{C}
is the nerve of an exact 1-category, then the map
\widehat{\ell}
in (
2.d

A proof of
Proposition

2.5

\infty
-categories are mapping spaces.

(2.e)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Extcat^{n}_{\mathscr{D}}(\mathscr{D},\mathscr{D})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\map_{\mathscr{D}}(\mathscr{D},\Sigma^{n}\mathscr{D})}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\phi}

Proof.

We have defined
{\map_{\mathscr{D}}(\mathscr{D},\Sigma^{n}\mathscr{D})}
as a pullback, as displayed on the right in the following diagram

(2.f)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Extcat_{\mathscr{D}}^{n}(\mathscr{D},\mathscr{D})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\map_{\mathscr{D}}(\mathscr{D},\Sigma^{n}\mathscr{D})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\map(\Delta^{1},\mathscr{D})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{D}\times\mathscr{D}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{D}\times\mathscr{D}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\epsilon_{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\phi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{eval}_{0}\times\mathrm{eval}_{1}}

The following corollaries will be immediately follow.

Corollary 3.4
.

Let
\mathscr{C}
be an exact
\infty
-category.
For every pair
(b,a)
of objects in
\mathscr{C}
, the sequence

\Extcat_{\mathscr{C}}(b,a)\coloneqq\{\Extcat^{n}_{\mathscr{C}}(b,a)\}_{n\geq 0}

is an
\Omega
-spectrum.

Corollary 3.5
.

The
(-n)
-th homotopy group of
\Extcat_{\mathscr{C}}(b,a)
is naturally isomorphic to
\pi_{0}\Extcat_{\mathscr{C}}^{n}(b,a)
.

\mathrm{D}^{b}(\mathcal{C})

Remark 3.9
.

The proof of
Lemma

3.8
closely resembles Klemenc’ proof that an exact
\infty
-category is extension closed in its stable hull

18
, Proposition 4.25]

by the universal property of the pullback. A simplicial 1-sphere has been filled. We only relied on universal properties, whence on can use the same type of argument to fill higher dimensional spheres.

Any object in
\classExtcat^{n}_{\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{st}}_{\geq 0}(\mathscr{C})}(\mathscr{C},\mathscr{C})
is weakly equivalent to an object in
\classExtcat^{n}_{\mathscr{C}}(\mathscr{C},\mathscr{C})
. Indeed, one uses
Lemma

3.8
to construct it, as shown in the diagram below. The diagram is supposed to read from right to left, and then from bottom to top. Objects denoted by minuscule letters are in
\mathscr{C}
and those represented by capital letters need not be.
In the last step, we use that
\mathscr{C}
is closed under extensions in
\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{st}}_{\geq 0}(\mathscr{C})
; thus
e_{1}\in\mathscr{C}
.

We are now ready to prove the main theorem.

.

Proof.

The natural transformation (
3.i
) should be defined in terms of a map of the bifibrations that make up its components.
Consider the homotopy pullback diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P^{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{C}\times\mathscr{C}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Extcat^{n}_{\mathscr{D}}(\mathscr{D},\mathscr{D})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{D}\times\mathscr{D}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{\epsilon_{n}^{\mathscr{D}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F\times F}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e_{n}^{\mathscr{D}}}

where the bottom row is the bifibration
\mathrm{eval}_{0}\times\mathrm{eval}_{n}
.
The functor
\widehat{\epsilon_{n}^{\mathscr{D}}}
is then a bifibration corresponding to the bifunctor
\Extcat_{\mathscr{D}}(F-,F-)
. An appropriate morphism of fibrations is now induced by the universal property of pullbacks, as displayed in the diagram below.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Extcat^{n}_{\mathscr{C}}(\mathscr{C},\mathscr{C})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P^{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{C}\times\mathscr{C}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Extcat^{n}_{\mathscr{D}}(\mathscr{D},\mathscr{D})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{D}\times\mathscr{D}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\epsilon_{n}^{\mathscr{C}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Extcat^{n}\!F}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{e^{\mathscr{D}}_{n}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F\times F}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\epsilon_{n}^{\mathscr{D}}}

Here, the map
\Extcat^{n}F
is the induced map established by
Proposition

2.7
.
The proof is complete.
∎

It has recently been shown that
\homcat\mathscr{C}
has a natural extriangulated structure when equipped with the bifunctor
\pi_{-1}\Extcat_{\mathscr{C}}
as well as a readily accessible additive realisation
[
25
, Theorem 4.22]
. In this section, we make use of the Retakh Ext-
\Omega
-spectrum to shed new light on Nakaoka–Palu’s result. More specifically, our claim is that the Retakh spectrum determines the extriangulation of the homotopy category as well as extriangulated functors between them. We will also prove in
Theorem

4.8
that higher extension categories induce the higher extension groups when passing to the homotopy category.

We need a few preliminary definitions to review the relatively novel theory of extriangulated categories.

\mathbf{E}
-extensions, it is quickly checked that there is a category of such. We denote this by

between homotopy categories is an extriangulated functor.

An extriangulated category is
topological
if it is equivalent to the homotopy category of some exact
\infty
-category.

We noted above that we have a natural isomorphism of bifunctors

\pi_{-1}\Extcat_{\mathscr{C}}\Longrightarrow\pi_{0}\Extcat_{\mathscr{C}}^{1}.

A realisation of
\pi_{-1}\Extcat_{\mathscr{C}}(-,-)
is achieved by precomposing the realisation
\iota_{\mathscr{C}}
with the equivalence
\Phi
from (
4.a
). It now follows from
Lemma

4.2
that the identity functor
1_{\homcat\mathscr{C}}
on
\homcat\mathscr{C}
yields an extriangulated equivalence

to itself, it is easy to see that the diagram commutes, and consequently that
\homcat F
is an extriangulated functor.

Klemenc’ embedding theorem (restated here as
Theorem

1.6
), as well as the discussion above, proves that any small topological extriangulated category embeds into a triangulated category.

As a new contribution, we generalise
Theorem

4.7
. The spectrum objects
\Extcat_{\mathscr{C}}(b,a)
do not only determine a natural extriangulation on
\homcat\mathscr{C}
. They also induce the higher extension functors, recently defined by Gorsky–Nakaoka–Palu
[
13
, Definition 3.1]
. We review their definition first.

. For a fixed pair of objects
(x,y)
, consider the bifunctor
S\coloneqq G(-,y)\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}F(x,-)
. Using the coend of
G
and
F
, one defines
G\diamond F
as follows:

(G\diamond F)(x,y)\coloneqq\int\limits^{c\in\mathcal{C}}G(c,y)\underset{\mathbb{Z}}{\otimes}F(x,c).

Since the category of abelian groups is cocomplete, the coend of a bifunctor
S
can be obtained as the coequaliser of the diagram

(4.b)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\coprod\limits_{f\colon c_{2}\rightarrow c_{1}}S(c_{2},c_{1})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod\limits_{c}S(c,c),}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod{S(c_{2},f)}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod{S(f,c_{1})}}

where the first coproduct is indexed over all morphisms in
\mathcal{C}
, and the second over all its objects.

Let
(\mathscr{C},\mathbf{E},\mathfrak{s})
be an extriangulated category. We set the zeroth extension functor to be the Hom-functor
\hom_{\mathcal{C}}(-,-)
, and the first to be
\mathbf{E}
.
The higher extension functors
\mathbf{E}^{\diamond n}
are then defined inductively by the formula
[
13
, Definition 3.1]

\mathbf{E}^{\diamond n}\coloneqq\mathbf{E}^{\diamond n-1}\diamond\mathbf{E}.

This section is concluded with its main result.

such that
m=\overline{m}\circ c_{b,a}\circ(\varphi^{n}_{c,a}\otimes 1)
, and then show that
\overline{m}
is unique. Let
\overline{m}(\mathbb{E})\coloneqq m(\widetilde{\mathbb{E}})
, where
\widetilde{\mathbb{E}}
is a choice of preimage of
\mathbb{E}
in
\coprod\limits_{c}S(c,c)
. This is a well-defined homomorphism; a different choice of preimage would yields the same result. The uniqueness of
\overline{m}
is a direct consequence of the fact that
c_{b,a}\circ(\varphi^{n}_{c,a}\otimes 1)
is an epimorphism.
∎

Appendix A
Proofs of diagram lemmas

We ended
Section

1
with a series of diagram lemmas for exact categories, claiming that they generalise to exact
\infty
-categories. These results are found in Bühler’s monograph
[
8
]
, as well as countless other texts. The proofs presented here are in an
\infty
-categorical context. Unlike the special case of exact 1-categories, cofibrations (resp. fibrations) are not necessarily monomorphisms (resp. epimorphisms) in a general
\infty
-categorical context.

Lemma
1.10
.

Consider a map of exact sequences
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces d}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i_{a}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{b}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i_{c}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{d}}

If
f^{\prime}
and
f^{\prime\prime}
are homotopy equivalences (resp. cofibrations, resp fibrations), so is
f
.

Proof.

If
f^{\prime}
and
f^{\prime\prime}
are homotopy equivalences, we use
Lemma

1.9
to construct a diagram
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces d}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces d}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i_{a}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\square}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{b}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\square}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i_{c}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p_{d}}

with exact rows. Since pushouts and pullbacks of homotopy equivalences are homotopy equivalences, the maps
g
and
h
are homotopy equivalences, whence
f=hg
is.

If
f^{\prime}
and
f^{\prime\prime}
are cofibrations, then
g
is a cofibration since it is a pushout of
f^{\prime}
, and
h
is a cofibration as a direct consequence of
(Ex3)
. Thus, the composite
f=h\circ g
is a cofibration.

If
f^{\prime}
and
f^{\prime\prime}
are fibrations, it is shown dually that
f
is a fibration.
∎

Lemma
1.11
.

Consider the commutative diagram with exact columns

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces e^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b^{\prime}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g^{\prime\prime}}

If the middle row and one of the other rows is exact, then the remaining row is exact.

Proof.

We assume that the top and middle rows are exact, and show that the bottom row is. The other case is dual.

The map of exact sequences connecting the top and middle rows can be factored

as asserted by
